title: St Patrick's Day
when_text: 17 March, the day Patrick is said to have died; a public holiday in Ireland and Northern Ireland
intro: Patrick was a Briton carried off to Ireland as a slave at sixteen who came back as a missionary bishop in the 5th century; his own Confessio is one of the few sure sources for his life. His feast became part of the Church's calendar in the 1600s, and parades, green and the shamrock came later still, many of them shaped by the Irish abroad. The places of his legend, from Slemish to Croagh Patrick and Lough Derg, are still walked by pilgrims.

facts.title: A slave who wrote his own story
facts.text: Two Latin writings by Patrick survive, the Confessio and a letter to the soldiers of Coroticus. In the Confessio he tells how Irish pirates took him from his home in Britain at sixteen and brought him to Ireland as a slave.

sources.title: Saint Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Two Latin writings by Patrick survive: the Confessio and the Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus.

sources.title: Saint Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Patrick writes that when he was sixteen, he was captured by Irish pirates from his home in Britain and taken as a slave to Ireland.

facts.title: A shepherd on Slemish
facts.text: Patrick does not name where he was held, but his 7th-century biographer Muirchú placed it at Slemish in County Antrim, where tradition says he herded sheep for six years. Crowds climb the hill on St Patrick's Day.

sources.title: Saint Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: However, Patrick's hagiographer Muirchú said it was in the area of Slemish mountain (Sliabh Mis) in Ulster.

sources.title: Slemish (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Saint Patrick's Day (17 March) large crowds walk to the top of the mountain as a pilgrimage.

facts.title: A church in a barn
facts.text: Tradition says Patrick's boat landed near Saul in County Down in 432, and the local chief Díchu, once converted, gave him a barn for a church. The village's name comes from the Old Irish word for barn.

sources.title: Saul, County Down (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The local chieftain, Dichu Mac Trichim, was converted and gave him a barn (Old Irish saball, hence the placename) for holding services.

facts.title: The Easter fire on the Hill of Slane
facts.text: Muirchú tells that Patrick lit an Easter fire on the Hill of Slane in defiance of the king at Tara, who had banned all fires while his own festival fire burned. Historians think the story moved to Slane a fire lit somewhere else.

sources.title: Hill of Slane (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: 433 in defiance of the High King Laoire who forbid any other fires while a festival fire was burning on the Hill of Tara.

sources.title: Hill of Slane (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Historians and archaeologists agree that Muirchu has moved to Slane a fire lit elsewhere

facts.title: No snakes to banish
facts.text: Ireland has had no snakes since the Ice Age, as the Roman writer Solinus already noted in the 3rd century. The story that Patrick drove them out is first written down by Jocelyn of Furness in the late 12th century.

sources.title: Saint Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: section Patrick banishes snakes from Ireland
sources.quote: Post-glacial Ireland never had snakes.

sources.title: Saint Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: section Patrick banishes snakes from Ireland
sources.quote: The earliest writings about Patrick ridding Ireland of snakes are by Jocelyn of Furness in the late twelfth century

facts.title: The shamrock and the Trinity
facts.text: Patrick is said to have used the three-leaved shamrock to explain the Trinity. Green ribbons and shamrocks have been worn on the day since at least the 1680s, and at the end of the day the shamrock was "drowned" in a glass of whiskey, beer or cider.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Saint Patrick is said to have used the shamrock, a three-leaved plant, to explain the Holy Trinity to the pagan Irish.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Green ribbons and shamrocks have been worn on Saint Patrick's Day since at least the 1680s.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: At the end of the celebrations, especially in Ireland, a shamrock is put into the bottom of a cup, which is then filled with whiskey, beer, or cider.

facts.title: St Patrick's blue
facts.text: Green was not always the saint's colour: the Order of St Patrick, founded in 1783, chose blue, and blue is still linked with him.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Order of St Patrick, an Anglo-Irish chivalric order founded in 1783, instead adopted blue as its colour, which led to blue being associated with Saint Patrick.

facts.title: A cathedral dedicated on the day
facts.text: St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, raised beside a holy well of the saint, was dedicated to God, Mary and St Patrick on 17 March 1191. It is the largest church in Ireland.

sources.title: St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The church was dedicated to "God, our Blessed Lady Mary and St Patrick" on 17 March 1191.

sources.title: St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the largest church in Ireland, was built between 1191 and 1270

facts.title: Into the Church's calendar
facts.text: Patrick's feast was only placed on the Catholic Church's universal calendar in the early 1600s, thanks to the Waterford-born Franciscan scholar Luke Wadding. Falling in Lent, it became a day when the fast and the ban on drink were lifted.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Saint Patrick's feast day was finally placed on the liturgical calendar of the Catholic Church in the early 1600s, due to the influence of Waterford-born Franciscan scholar Luke Wadding.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Historically, the Lenten restrictions on fasting and drinking alcohol were lifted for the day, which has encouraged the holiday's tradition of revelry.

facts.title: Parades came home late
facts.text: St Patrick's Day parades began among the Irish in North America in the 18th century (the day was marked in what is now the United States from 1600). Ireland's first parade was in Waterford in 1903, the year the day became a public holiday; Dublin's first official parade was in 1931.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Saint Patrick's Day parades began in North America in the 18th century but did not spread to Ireland until the 20th century.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first Saint Patrick's Day parade in Ireland was held in Waterford in 1903, hundreds of years after the first parade in North America.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first official, state-sponsored Saint Patrick's Day parade in Dublin took place in 1931.

facts.title: Shamrock for the Irish Guards
facts.text: Since Queen Alexandra began it in 1901, a member of the royal family has presented bowls of fresh shamrock, flown in from Ireland, to the Irish Guards on St Patrick's Day.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: following Queen Alexandra introducing the tradition in 1901

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Fresh Shamrocks are presented to the Irish Guards, regardless of where they are stationed, and are flown in from Ireland.

facts.title: Reek Sunday is in July
facts.text: Croagh Patrick, where Patrick is said to have fasted for forty days, is climbed by thousands not on 17 March but on Reek Sunday, the last Sunday in July, some of them barefoot. A custom at least as old as the Middle Ages; a stone oratory stood on the summit from the 5th century.

sources.title: Croagh Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Croagh Patrick is climbed by thousands of pilgrims every year on Reek Sunday, the last Sunday in July, a custom which goes back to at least the Middle Ages.

sources.title: Croagh Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Archaeologists found that there had been a stone chapel or oratory on the summit since the 5th century.

sources.title: Saint Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: section Patrick's fast on the mountain
sources.quote: Tírechán wrote in the 7th century that Patrick spent forty days on the mountaintop of Cruachán Aigle

facts.title: A doorway to Purgatory
facts.text: Legend says Christ showed Patrick a cave on Station Island in Lough Derg that led into Purgatory. Mentioned in texts from 1185 and marked on maps across Europe, it still draws pilgrims each summer, who go barefoot and keep an all-night vigil.

sources.title: St Patrick's Purgatory (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Its importance in medieval times is clear from the fact that it is mentioned in texts from as early as 1185 and shown on maps from all over Europe as early as the fifteenth century.

sources.title: St Patrick's Purgatory (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Pilgrims spend the first night in the island's basilica in prayer, and only on the second night can they finally sleep in the dormitory.

facts.title: A grave stone of 1900
facts.text: Patrick is said to have died on 17 March and to be buried at Downpatrick. The inscribed granite stone that marks his grave beside Down Cathedral was only put there in 1900.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Tradition holds that he died on 17 March and was buried at Downpatrick.

sources.title: Down Cathedral (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: However, the inscribed stone of Mourne granite allegedly marking the grave was actually put in place in 1900.

places.name: Down Cathedral
places.why: Church of Ireland cathedral in Downpatrick; Patrick's traditional grave is in its grounds, and the town holds one of the largest St Patrick's Day celebrations outside the cities.

sources.title: Down Cathedral (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In the cathedral grounds is the burial place of St Patrick, believed to have died in 461.

sources.title: Saint Patrick's Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: One of the biggest celebrations outside the cities is in Downpatrick, County Down, where Saint Patrick is said to be buried.

places.name: Saul, County Down
places.why: Where Patrick is said to have held services in a gifted barn and, by tradition, to have died; Saint Patrick's Memorial Church with its replica round tower stands on the reputed spot.

sources.title: Saul, County Down (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The modern "Saint Patrick's Memorial Church" is built on the reputed spot of this building and includes a replica round tower.

sources.title: Saul, County Down (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Allegedly, Saint Patrick died in Saul Monastery on 17 March 461 and is buried in nearby Downpatrick.

places.name: Slemish
places.why: Hill in County Antrim where tradition says the young Patrick tended sheep as a slave; climbed by crowds on 17 March.

sources.title: Slemish (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Tradition holds that Saint Patrick, enslaved as a youth, was brought to this area and tended sheep herds on Slemish, and that during this time he found God.

places.name: Hill of Slane
places.why: Hilltop church and college ruins where Muirchú set Patrick's defiant Easter fire, in sight of Tara; Patrick is more surely said to have made Erc bishop of Slane.

sources.title: Hill of Slane (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Hill of Slane can be seen from the Hill of Tara which is about 16 kilometres (9.9 mi) away.

sources.title: Hill of Slane (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is somewhat more certain that Patrick appointed a bishop of Slane, Saint Erc.

places.name: St Patrick's Cathedral, Armagh (Church of Ireland)
places.why: Stands where tradition says Patrick founded his main church in 445; Brian Boru was buried here after Clontarf in 1014.

sources.title: St Patrick's Cathedral, Armagh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: According to tradition, a church was founded on the site in 445 by Saint Patrick.

sources.title: St Patrick's Cathedral, Armagh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Brian was buried at Armagh cathedral after his death at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014.

places.name: St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin
places.why: Dedicated on St Patrick's Day 1191 beside a holy well of the saint; its door with a hole cut in 1492 is the legendary origin of "chancing your arm".

sources.title: St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: beside a holy well of the same name and on an island between two branches of the River Poddle

sources.title: St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Legend has it that Saint Patrick's was the place where the expression "chancing your arm" (meaning to take a risk) originated

places.name: Croagh Patrick
places.why: Holy mountain in Mayo named after the saint, with a summit chapel of 1905 on the site of a 5th-century oratory; pilgrims climb on the last Sunday in July.

sources.title: Croagh Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A small modern chapel was built on the summit and dedicated on 20 July 1905.

sources.title: Croagh Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: On the last Sunday in July, thousands of pilgrims climb Croagh Patrick in honour of Saint Patrick, and masses are held at the summit chapel.

places.name: Ballintubber Abbey
places.why: Start of Tóchar Phádraig, the old pilgrim path to Croagh Patrick, revived as a 30 km walk of about ten hours.

sources.title: Croagh Patrick (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Originally, most pilgrims climbed the mountain from the east, following the Togher Patrick (Tochár Phádraig) pilgrim path from Ballintubber Abbey.

places.name: St Patrick's Purgatory, Station Island
places.why: Island in Lough Derg with the legendary cave to Purgatory; a pilgrimage site since the Middle Ages, open to pilgrims from early June to 15 August.

sources.title: St Patrick's Purgatory (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: St Patrick's Purgatory is an ancient pilgrimage site on Station Island in Lough Derg, County Donegal, Ireland.

sources.title: St Patrick's Purgatory (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Every year the main pilgrimage season begins in late May/early June and ends mid-August, on the 15th, the feast of the Assumption of Mary.

places.name: Library of Trinity College Dublin
places.why: Holds the 9th-century Book of Armagh, with early texts about Patrick, including the lives by Tírechán and Muirchú.

sources.title: Book of Armagh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is held by the Library of Trinity College Dublin (MS 52).

sources.title: Book of Armagh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The document is valuable for containing early texts relating to St Patrick, the 7th century Irish bishop Tírechán, the Irish monk Muirchú.
